title: Story of the Sage and the Scholar

keywords: story of the sage and the scholar
full_text:
A proud young scholar from Al-Azhar University, puffed up with arrogance from memorizing ten thousand verses of poetry and theological texts, sought out the famous desert ascetic Sage Abu Ishaq.

Finding the sage watering a neglected pomegranate bush outside his mud-brick cell, the young scholar bowed perfunctorily and began to lecture:
'O Master, I have mastered the seven schools of grammar, the intricacies of inheritance law, the disputes of logic, and the commentaries of philosophy. I have come that thou mayest examine me and declare me the leading scholar of Cairo.'

Abu Ishaq continued watering the thirsty plant, then said gently:
'Fetch me a bowl of fresh milk from the peasant woman in yonder hut.'

The scholar went and brought back a shallow wooden bowl filled to the brim with goat's milk.
'Now,' said the sage, 'carry this bowl three times around the entire perimeter of our village without spilling a single drop. If thou spillest even one bead, thy learning is void.'

The scholar lifted the bowl carefully, walking with tense, rigid steps. He focused his eyes solely on the white surface, sweating under the afternoon sun, balancing the liquid with intense concentration.
He returned triumphant: 'Behold, Master! I walked the entire circuit, and not a single drop was spilled!'

Abu Ishaq looked at him calmly:
'While walking through the village, didst thou notice the blind orphan crying by the ditch?'
'No,' replied the scholar. 'I looked only at the milk.'
'Didst thou see the poor laborer struggling under a fallen timber?'
'No, I was guarding the bowl!'
'Didst thou hear the greetings of peace offered by the village elders?'
'I could hear nothing, for fear of losing a drop!'

Abu Ishaq shook his head with sorrowful smile:
'Thou hast carried a bowl of milk, but missed the entire world.
Thy books have taught thee to balance words, but have blinded thee to the suffering, joy, and reality of thy fellow men. Go, throw away thy arrogance. Learn to see the orphan, help the laborer, and return the elder's greeting. For learning that does not blossom into kindness is nothing more than vanity.'

The young scholar lowered his head in shame, kissed the sage's rough hand, and began his true education in humility and service.
moral: Book knowledge without compassionate practice is like a donkey laden with books; true learning lives in conduct.
